title: The third day
hook: the resurrection is the hinge of Christian faith (1 Corinthians 15:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was he descended: broken doors, and Adam and Eve lifted by the wrists. Your line was even there.

A church is starting to wobble. Some of its members have begun saying there's no such thing as rising from the dead. Maybe Jesus's resurrection is just a lovely way of talking. A letter writer could soften it: even without it, the teaching is still beautiful, the example still inspiring. Paul, writing to that church in Corinth, does the opposite. He puts everything on the table. In effect, he says: if this didn't happen, the whole thing falls. Every sermon, every prayer, every hope. He calls it vain. Empty. Today's word is the line in the creed that everything hangs on. After he descended, the creed says: the third day he rose again from the dead.
screen: `A CHURCH STARTING TO WOBBLE.` → `PAUL DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` → `EVERYTHING HANGS HERE.`

segments.voice: In First Corinthians 15, Paul says he's passing on what he himself received, a short summary he didn't make up: "that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures." Then he lists who saw him: Peter, the twelve, more than five hundred people at once, most of them still alive, Paul adds, as if to say, go and ask them. James. And last of all, Paul himself. Then the hinge: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." The New Testament doesn't tell it as a nice metaphor for spring, or for the teaching living on. The Gospels tell of an empty tomb found by women at dawn, and a risen Jesus who can be touched, who eats fish, who still carries his wounds, and yet is changed, sometimes not recognized at first. The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds both confess it. Some modern Christian thinkers have read it more spiritually; the creeds speak of a rising from the dead, and the conversation goes on. The Greek word is anastasis, standing up again. All through the Easter season, Orthodox Christians greet each other with three words, Christ is risen, and the answer, He is risen indeed. Death is not the end: that's the claim the whole faith hangs on.
screen: `WHAT PAUL RECEIVED.` · `FIVE HUNDRED AT ONCE: GO ASK THEM.` · `THE HINGE: IF NOT, IT'S VAIN.` · `ANASTASIS: STANDING UP AGAIN.` · then, large: `HE ROSE AGAIN THE THIRD DAY.`

segments.voice: Picture the garden in the dark before dawn, from the Easter chapters, Mark 16 or John 20: the stone, the women walking with spices, what they expected to find, and what they found instead. In John, Mary Magdalene meets the gardener, and he says her name. If you pray, pray the old Easter greeting, Christ is risen; if you don't, stay with the women in the garden, in that moment of surprise.
Anastasis. The Greek word for resurrection, standing up again: Christ risen on the third day, and everything hanging on it.
Your line: death is not the end. Christ is risen; he is risen indeed. That's day three hundred four.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter, and Sunday, the day the Gospels name for the empty tomb, is kept as a little Easter; Orthodox Christians greet each other with "Christ is risen" through the Easter season.

original.note: Greek: standing up again, resurrection. Also the name of the Orthodox Easter icon.

trapdoor: what you thought: Easter is about spring and new beginnings.
what it means: Christians say Jesus truly rose from the dead on the third day, and the whole faith hangs on it.
what a scholar hears: 1 Corinthians 15:3–7, a formula Paul says he received and handed on, with a list of witnesses he invites readers to check.

notes: 1 Corinthians dated c. 53–55; script says 'around twenty-five years after Jesus died'. Confirm.
The early date of the 1 Cor 15:3–7 formula (within a few years of the crucifixion) is a widely held scholarly view; script says 'scholars think... may go back'.
The Apostles' Creed line 'The third day he rose again from the dead' is given in the hook without quotation marks. Confirm acceptable.
Spiritual vs bodily readings noted without ranking; confirm wording 'some modern Christian thinkers'.
Orthodox paschal greeting: 'Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!' (Christos anesti / Alithos anesti); script renders the reply as 'He is risen indeed', the common English form.
